(Dakota News Now) - As the weather gets cooler, bats will be looking for a warmer place to roost, which could bring them closer to homes and pets. Animal control officials say knowing how to respond could help protect pets from a potentially dangerous encounter. While bat encounters can be concerning, animal control said the numbers show rabies-positive bats are still relatively uncommon. So far this year, Animal Control has responded to 365 bat calls, and 62 of those bats were sent in for rabies testing, said Patty Beckman, Sioux Falls Animal Control supervisor. Only two of those bats have come back positive for the rabies virus. “So not all bats have the rabies virus,” Beckman said. Officials said it can be difficult to tell if a bat is carrying the virus just by looking at it or watching its behavior. “It’s not easy to just look at a bat and its behavior to say, ‘Oh, that’s a rabid bat,’” said Hilary Ward, South Dakota State University assistant professor and veterinary pathologist. That’s why officials say any possible contact should be taken seriously. If a bat scratches, bites, or lands on a person, or comes into contact with a pet, the bat can be sent for testing. “Known contact would be if a bat bites you, if a bat lands on you, if you feel like a bat scratched you—anything like that where a bat would even touch you, and you feel like you had contact, we can definitely send it in for rabies testing,” Beckman said. Pets don’t have to spend time outside to be at risk. “It is very important even for your animals that are strictly indoors to be rabies vaccinated, just in case if a bat would get into your house and they would have contact with that bat,” Beckman said. Ward said rabies is a serious disease and testing can determine whether an exposure occurred. “As a veterinary professional, we are going to err on the side of caution to say, if you’ve had a bat in your home, we recommend that you have that bat tested,” Ward said. Officials say keeping up to date on pet rabies vaccinations is one of the best ways to protect them. If a pet comes into contact with a bat, officials say to reach out to a veterinarian or animal control. Copyright 2026 Dakota News Now. All rights reserved. Boehringer Ingelheim and AWARE launch new Stop Rabies project in Zimbabwe to help protect dogs and communities Boehringer Ingelheim Wed, September 23, 2026 at 4:00 AM EDT 4 min read Boehringer Ingelheim Boehringer headquarters Ingelheim, Germany Rabies remains one of the world's deadliest yet preventable zoonotic diseases, highlighting the need for sustained prevention efforts. Through a new multi-year collaboration, Boehringer Ingelheim and AWARE are expanding dog vaccination, population management and education efforts in rural Zimbabwe. By protecting animal health, the initiative helps safeguard people, communities, and livelihoods. Ingelheim, Germany – As part of its global Stop Rabies program, Boehringer Ingelheim, AWARE Germany e.V. and AWARE Trust Zimbabwe are launching a comprehensive rabies-control initiative in the Tsholotsho District of Zimbabwe, one of the most remote and poorest rural areas in the country. Together, the two veterinary-led AWARE organizations follow a holistic One-Health approach to improve animal welfare, community wellbeing, and wildlife conservation. The collaboration with Boehringer Ingelheim combines dog vaccination and population management with education of children to help reduce the burden of rabies in one of the country's most affected regions. Rabies is entirely preventable, yet it continues to claim tens of thousands of lives every year. Rural communities are especially vulnerable, and children are among those most affected. Because more than 99% of human rabies cases originate from infected dogs, vaccinating dogs remains the most effective way to stop the disease at its source and protect both people and animals1. Expanding Stop Rabies in Zimbabwe At the center of the new Stop Rabies project in Zimbabwe is a comprehensive program based at AWARE's veterinary hub in Tsholotsho. Through mobile veterinary teams, the project aims to vaccinate approximately 15,000 dogs every year, reaching an estimated vaccination coverage of more than 90% of the local dog population. The program also includes the free sterilization of at least 1,200 dogs annually, helping support sustainable rabies control and animal welfare. "No one should die from a disease that can be prevented. Through our Stop Rabies program, we are contributing to eliminating dog-mediated human rabies deaths, knowing that this can only be achieved through collective action," says Thaïs Vila, Global Program Lead for Stop Rabies at Boehringer Ingelheim. The collaboration builds on AWARE's longstanding rabies prevention work in Zimbabwe and reflects a shared commitment to protecting interconnected lives. Protecting dogs from rabies is one of the most effective ways to reduce disease transmission, improve human health and strengthen community resilience. Story Continues "We have seen firsthand how sustained vaccination, and community engagement can reduce the burden of rabies. With Boehringer Ingelheim's support, we can expand our reach and strengthen local veterinary services to help protect even more communities across Tsholotsho," says Martin Kessler, Chair of AWARE Germany. Education is another key part of the collaboration. AWARE is expanding its PAWS Clubs (Promoting Animal Welfare Clubs), training 170 teachers across 85 schools and reaching more than 50,000 students with information on rabies prevention, safe interactions with dogs and responsible animal care. Through this collaboration, Boehringer Ingelheim and AWARE are demonstrating how collective action can help protect lives and move communities closer to a future free from dog-mediated rabies. By combining prevention, education and community action, the partnership is helping tackle rabies at its source while building a model that can support long-term progress in affected communities. 1 World Health Organization (WHO). Rabies. https://www.who.int/health-topics/rabies About AWARE AWARE Trust Zimbabwe and AWARE Germany e.V. are partner non-governmental organizations dedicated to protecting biodiversity through veterinary outreach, education and wildlife conservation programs. Both organizations are led by veterinarians and work closely with local communities to improve the health and wellbeing of animals, people and ecosystems. Learn more at www.aware-germany.de Boehringer Ingelheim – Animal Health business Boehringer Ingelheim provides innovation for preventing and treating diseases in animals. The company offers a wide range of vaccines, parasite-control products, and medicines for pets, horses, and livestock to veterinarians, animal owners, farmers, and governments. As a leader in animal health, Boehringer Ingelheim values that the health of humans and animals is deeply connected and strives to make a difference for people, animals, and society. Learn more at www.boehringer-ingelheim.com/animal-health. Boehringer Ingelheim Boehringer Ingelheim is a biopharmaceutical company active in both human and animal health. As one of the industry's top investors in research and development, the company focuses on developing innovative therapies that can improve and extend lives in areas of high unmet medical need. Independent since its foundation in 1885, Boehringer takes a long-term perspective, embedding sustainability along the entire value chain. Our approximately 54,300 employees serve over 130 markets to build a healthier and more sustainable tomorrow. Learn more at www.boehringer-ingelheim.com. (Photo: PIA-10) CAGAYAN de Oro City — A bite or scratch from an animal should not be treated at home alone, as the Department of Health in Northern Mindanao is reminding the public that quick medical attention can prevent rabies from becoming fatal. Dr. John Daniel Estandarte, medical officer III of the DOH NorthMin Infectious Diseases Cluster, urged people exposed to potentially infected animals to wash the wound immediately and seek treatment at an accredited Animal Bite Treatment Center. “Wash with soap and water, diretso na dayon ka sa mga Animal Bite Treatment Center,” Estandarte said during the Talakayan sa PIA: Konsultayo Series on Sept. 4 at SM CDO Uptown. What to do after a bite DOH advises people with animal bite or scratch wounds to: Wash the wound with soap and running water for 10 to 15 minutes. Go immediately to an Animal Bite Treatment Center for assessment. Follow the recommended post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) treatment schedule. Avoid relying on unverified traditional remedies such as pagtatandok or wound suctioning in place of medical care. Estandarte said dogs account for 95% to 99% of human rabies cases, making prompt assessment important after exposure. He also said bites or scratches involving the head and neck are considered particularly high-risk because the rabies virus attacks the nervous system. Injuries to highly innervated areas such as the hands and face also require prompt medical assessment. “Ang gina-atake sa rabies virus kay ang utok, [anywhere] above the neck, mao na siya ang high risk kaayo,” Estandarte said. Don’t stop treatment early People who have already started PEP but missed a scheduled dose or failed to complete the recommended treatment should return to an accredited Animal Bite Treatment Center, Estandarte said. Health workers can assess the person’s exposure and provide guidance on the next steps. The DOH continues to train health workers and accredit Animal Bite Treatment Centers to improve access to PEP in Northern Mindanao. It also works with the Bureau of Animal Industry and local partners on mass pet vaccination and responsible pet ownership to help prevent rabies transmission. Rabies is preventable through timely post-exposure care, but once symptoms develop, the disease is almost always fatal. (With a report Rushen Mae N. content: By Felicia Imohimi The Federal Government says it will commence free anti-rabies vaccination of dogs in Gwagwalada, Kubwa and other parts of the country on Saturday, Sept. 26. Dr Samuel Anzaku, Chief Veterinary Officer of Nigeria (CVON) and Director, Veterinary Public Health and Epidemiology, Federal Ministry of Livestock Development (FMLD), said this on Friday in Abuja. Anzaku spoke during a road walk organised to commemorate the 2026 World Rabies Day (WRD), marked annually on Sept. 28. The 2026 commemoration is themed “Stronger Together” The road work was aimed at public enlightenment on rabies prevention, reporting and vaccination. He said the intervention would be implemented by the Federal and state governments in collaboration with development partners, veterinarians and other stakeholders. Anzaku said the vaccination was aimed at reducing the burden of rabies and contributing to the global target of eliminating dog-mediated human rabies by 2030. He urged dog owners to take their pets to designated veterinary clinics for the free vaccination. He also announced plans to provide human pre-exposure prophylaxis to frontline workers who regularly come in contact with dogs. “Veterinarians, paraprofessionals, the hunters who are always in contact with these dogs will be given some pre-exposure prophylaxis against rabies, because you do not have to wait until this problem happens,” he said. Anzaku said the government had lined up activities to translate the World Rabies Day commemoration into concrete actions, especially through mass dog vaccination. “Through the mass vaccination we are targeting two or three area councils beginning from tomorrow,” he said. He described rabies as a preventable viral disease affecting warm-blooded animals, including humans, and said it could be transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, usually following a bite. “In Nigeria, dogs are the principal source of rabies infection in humans,” Anzaku said. He said this year’s WRD theme, “Stronger Together”, underscored the need for collaboration among dog owners, government institutions and other stakeholders. According to him, the One Health approach brings together the Ministries of Health, Environment and Livestock Development, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) and other stakeholders. He said the ministry was collaborating with the health and environment ministries, NCDC and World Against Rabies Foundation to raise awareness and strengthen preventive measures. Anzaku also urged the Ministry of Environment to intensify efforts to control stray dogs, describing them as a major contributor to the spread of rabies. He called for active community participation, including traditional rulers, local government chairmen, state governors, development partners and civil society organisations. “It is only through collective effort we will be able to overcome rabies. Prevention is better than cure. Take your dogs to the nearest veterinary clinic. “Report any bite to the nearest hospital so that immediate action can be taken,” he said. Dr George Onyemaowa, National Coordinator, Rabies Control Programme in Nigeria said the road walk was organised to raise awareness about rabies prevention and the need for immediate treatment after a dog bite. Onyemaowa, also the Coordinator, One Health Technical Working Group on Rabies urged members of the public to immediately wash dog-bite wounds with soap and water and proceed to the nearest hospital. Speaking on the prevalence of rabies, he said reports were being received from between 18 and 20 states monthly. “As it stands now, we have over 100 cases already between January and August. And almost every week we keep getting reports,” he said. Onyemaowa identified Plateau, Bauchi and Gombe as among the states reporting high numbers of rabies cases. He listed symptoms in humans to include fever, headache, pain or tingling around the bite, confusion, irritability, fear of water and paralysis, which could result in death. Dr Moses Arokoyo, President, Nigerian Veterinary Medical Association (NVMA), said the association was committed to supporting efforts to eradicate rabies. Arokoyo, represented by Dr Chinnaemeka Joe-Iruobe, Chairperson, FCT chapter of NVMA, said rabies deaths were distressing because the disease was preventable. “I follow the fight against rabies with passion as a veterinarian. If we can eradicate rabies by 2030, I will be the happiest person in the world,” he said. (NAN) FUA/TAK Edited by Tosin Kolade

The Stanislaus County Health Services Agency is hoping to raise awareness about rabies as World Rabies Day approaches. The health caution comes as Stanislaus County has recorded two confirmed cases of rabies in animals, a bat and a skunk, this year. Both of the animals that tested positive for rabies had interactions with domestic pets, reinforcing the importance of vaccinating pets and preventing them from interacting with wildlife, according to the health department. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also recently issued a Health Advisory following increases in reported human exposures to rabid or potentially rabid animals in several areas of the United States. “Rabies is rare, but it is an extremely serious disease that is nearly universally fatal once symptoms develop,” said Thea Papasozomenos, MD, MPH, Stanislaus County Public Health Officer. “The good news is that rabies is preventable. Avoid contact with wild animals, keep your pets vaccinated, and seek medical advice promptly if you think you or a family member may have been exposed.” In 2024, a Dos Palos teacher died after being bitten by a presumably rabid bat in Merced County approximately one month earlier. Deaths from rabies are rare in the United States, with fewer than 10 cases identified each year. Nonetheless, each year, thousands of people receive preventive treatment for rabies following a bite or other direct contact with an animal with possible rabies. Rabies is a viral disease that affects the brain and nervous system. Any mammal, including people and domestic animals, can become infected. In California, bats are the animal most frequently reported with rabies, followed by skunks. Rabies is usually transmitted through the bite of an infected animal but can also spread when infected saliva comes into contact with broken skin or the eyes, nose, or mouth. Once symptoms develop, rabies is nearly always fatal. However, rabies can be prevented when potential exposures are identified and appropriate medical care is received before symptoms develop. Residents should never touch, feed, capture, or attempt to care for wild animals, including those that appear sick or injured. This is especially important with bats because their bites can be small and may not leave an obvious mark. A bat found on the ground or active during the day may be sick or injured and should not be handled. Residents can reduce the risk of rabies by: Keeping pets vaccinated. Make sure pets are current on recommended rabies vaccinations. Avoiding contact with wildlife. Never handle or attempt to care for bats, skunks, or other wild animals. Supervising pets outdoors. Keep pets from approaching or interacting with wildlife. Teaching children to avoid wild or unfamiliar animals, even if an animal appears friendly, sick, or injured. Taking possible exposures seriously. Seek guidance after direct contact with a bat or other potentially rabid animal, even if you do not see an obvious bite. If you are bitten or scratched by a wild or unfamiliar animal, immediately wash the area thoroughly with soap and water and contact a healthcare provider. If you had direct contact with a bat or find a bat in a situation where contact cannot be ruled out, such as in a room with a sleeping person, unattended young child, or someone unable to reliably report whether contact occurred, contact a healthcare provider or Public Health for a rabies risk assessment. When recommended, rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is highly effective at preventing rabies when given before symptoms develop. If your pet has contact with a bat, skunk, or other potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian promptly. If a wild animal may have had contact with a person or pet, do not handle or release it before receiving guidance because the animal may need to be tested for rabies. For questions about possible human rabies exposure, contact Public Health at (209) 558-7700. For concerns involving wildlife or domestic animals, contact your local animal control agency. For more information about rabies, visit the California Department of Public Health or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention rabies webpages. An official said the case is part of a wider pattern of bat rabies activity across Oregon this year. As of July, 22 bats had tested positive for rabies in Oregon. People should avoid touching a dead or live bat with bare hands. There is no way to determine if a bat has rabies by appearance. "If you've touched a bat, woken up with a bat in your room, or aren't sure whether you were bitten or scratched, contact a healthcare provider or Linn County Health Services right away," a news release said. "If you are bitten or scratched, wash the area well with soap and water and get medical advice immediately." The rabies virus spreads from infected mammals to humans and is almost always fatal once symptoms appear, officials said. Rabies is preventable if people get medical care before symptoms begin. In Oregon, bats are the only wild species that naturally carries the rabies virus. Foxes, skunks, cats, dogs and other animals can become infected after contact with a rabid bat. Residents are asked to vaccinate dogs against rabies and instruct children to avoid bats and report them to adults. To report an exposure or ask questions, call Linn County Health Services at 541-967-3888 ext. 2488 or 541-750-0090 after business hours. Harford County launches rabies vaccination bait program | Exclusive WBAL US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 2:53 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 7:32 PM EDT Sep 23, 2026 Editorial Standards i Tommie Clark Reporter Harford County health officials deploy vaccination bait program amid rise in rabies cases Number of animals testing positive for rabies in Harford County already matches county's total for all of 2025 Updated: 7:32 PM EDT Sep 23, 2026 Editorial Standards i Tommie Clark Reporter BEL AIR, Md. — Rabies cases are increasing in Harford County, leading health officials to launch a pilot vaccination program to prevent the spread of the disease. | HARFORD COUNTY : Oral Rabies Vaccination Project Advertisement "Harford County is, unfortunately, (where there is) the highest number of rabid animals tested for the state of Maryland, so far," said Hannah Lux, a community hygiene supervisor at the Harford County Health Department. County health officials on Wednesday gave WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates an exclusive look at the vaccination program, which involves strategically placing more than 15,000 vaccine baits across the county. Wild raccoons bite into the bricks or packets and receive immunization. Harford County health officials say they're following the lead of Anne Arundel County's program . So far this year, as many as 28 animals have tested positive for rabies in Harford County, matching the county's total for all of 2025. Raccoons account for 18 of the cases, along with some foxes, groundhogs and bats. On Wednesday, county health officials announced another fox was confirmed to have tested positive for rabies. The fox was found near the 2300 block of Perry Avenue in Edgewood. "We're a little bit higher, but we're also testing a pretty good number of animals. So, the more animals you test, the more likely you are to have positives," Lux told WBAL-TV 11 News. According to data obtained by WBAL-TV 11 News Investigates, Harford County reported 23 rabies cases in 2024, 11 in 2023 and 21 in 2022. "If an animal has had contact with people or pets ... then we would want to test." Raymond, a county resident, shared his experience with rabid raccoons. "I see rabid raccoons all the time. I have one that comes around often enough, he has a name," Raymond told WBAL-TV 11 News. "I always keep my distance." Lux explained that while the numbers are slightly up, they remain in line with expectations as reports of animal exposures have increased nationwide. She emphasized the importance of awareness to help residents respond appropriately to encounters with rabid animals. | MORE : If exposed to rabies, what do you do? "If an animal has had contact with people or pets, like a bite or a scratch, then we would want to test," Lux told WBAL-TV 11 News. Health officials said witnessing a raccoon is not cause for alarm, but if you or your pets have had contact with infected animals, get tested and call the Harford County Health Department at 410-877-2300 for follow-up. Health officials offer the following tips to pet owners: Keep pets leashed when out for walks and closely monitor them while they're in the back yard. All cats, dogs and ferrets should remain up to date on their rabies vaccinations through their vet office or local rabies vaccination clinic. Cover trash cans and do not leave pet food outside. Avoid feeding, petting or interacting with wildlife in any way. Call Harford County Animal Control at 410-638-3505 when you see a stray animal showing abnormal behaviors, such as excessive affection, aggression, lethargy or disorientation. "It's a little spooky, I guess. Definitely unexpected. We play outside all the time, so hearing about rabies is always scary, especially when there's kids involved," said Chris McIntosh of Forest Hill. Neighbors in a Forest Hill community said they are concerned after a rabid groundhog was found in their neighborhood this week. That case was one of four rabies-positive animals reported in the county this week. A rabid groundhog and raccoon were reported from Aberdeen on Tuesday. "Surprising, I mean we've seen some foxes and some other stuff wandering around but having a rabid animal is always concerning," said Christian Taylor of Forest Hill. World Rabies Day 2026: Stronger Together against rabies Distributed by EIN Presswire This WRD, communities around the world are coming together under the theme “Stronger Together” to highlight the importance of collaboration to eliminate rabies. Stronger Together reminds us that eliminating rabies takes all of us. By sharing knowledge, coordinating efforts and supporting one another, we can build safer, healthier communities.” — Dr Andre Coetzer, GARC’s Chief Executive Officer. KS, UNITED STATES, September 22, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — This World Rabies Day, communities around the world are coming together under the theme “Stronger Together” to highlight the importance of working together to prevent and eliminate rabies. On 28 September 2026, individuals, communities, governments, healthcare workers, veterinary professionals, educators and organizations will come together to raise awareness about rabies and take action to protect both people and animals. This year’s theme reflects a simple but important truth: rabies elimination is only possible when we work together. Rabies is one of the world’s oldest and deadliest diseases, but it is also entirely preventable. Every year, an estimated 59 000 people die from rabies, with children making up almost half of those deaths. The tools to eliminate dog-mediated rabies already exist: Vaccinating dogs, educating communities, and ensuring that people exposed to rabies know what to do. “Stronger Together reminds us that no individual or organization can eliminate rabies alone,” says Dr Andre Coetzer, GARC’s Chief Executive Officer. “Whether you are a pet owner, a community volunteer, a veterinarian, a healthcare professional, a teacher or a policymaker, everyone has a role to play. When we share knowledge, coordinate our efforts and support one another, we can create safer, healthier communities for people and animals.” Around the world, people are marking World Rabies Day through vaccination campaigns, community outreach, school education programs, public awareness activities, fundraising events and social media campaigns. These efforts demonstrate the power of local action and the importance of partnerships in creating lasting change. GARC, Rabies Alliance initiated World Rabies Day in 2007, and we continue to support communities and organizations working towards rabies elimination. Through the GARC Data Platform, the GARC Education Platform, and the Communities Against Rabies program, we empower communities with the knowledge and skills they need to lead effective rabies elimination efforts. This World Rabies Day, everyone has a role to play. Pet owners can ensure their dogs and cats are vaccinated against rabies. Communities can share accurate information and support local vaccination campaigns. Parents and teachers can help children learn how to safely interact with animals and what to do if bitten. Organizations and governments need to work together to strengthen rabies elimination and response systems. GARC believes that collaboration is not optional but essential because every action matters. By working together, we can move closer to a world free from dog-mediated rabies. ENDS About World Rabies Day World Rabies Day is observed annually on 28 September to raise awareness about rabies prevention and highlight global efforts to eliminate the disease. Coordinated by the Global Alliance for Rabies Control, it has been endorsed by international human and veterinary health organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). About GARC, Rabies Alliance GARC, Rabies Alliance is a global non-profit organization committed to ending human and animal deaths from dog-mediated rabies. GARC works with communities, governments, veterinary and public health professionals, educators and other stakeholders to empower communities and support sustainable rabies elimination efforts. For more information about World Rabies Day 2026, visit World Rabies Day.
